blocks.text: Multi-task fine-tuning trains a single model on a mixture of several different task types at once, aiming for one deployed model that handles a family of related jobs well, rather than maintaining a separate task specific model for each individual job.

This topic covers the specific challenges that only appear once a dataset mixes multiple tasks together, task balance, transfer between tasks, and how to signal to the model which task it is handling at any given moment.
1. What Multi-Task Fine-Tuning Means Here

blocks.alt: Examples from task A, B, and C mix into one dataset

blocks.text: Rather than the single narrow dataset used in task specific fine-tuning, covered in the previous topic, a multi-task dataset deliberately combines examples from several distinct task types into one shared training set, teaching the model to handle all of them from a single set of weights.
2. Mixing Tasks Within One Training Dataset

Building a multi-task dataset means applying the same collection, cleaning, and formatting principles covered throughout the Dataset Fundamentals and Dataset Preparation modules to each individual task, then combining the results, rather than skipping careful preparation for any one task because it is only part of a larger mixture.
3. Task Balance, Avoiding One Task Dominating

blocks.alt: An overrepresented task and an underrepresented task both create an imbalance risk

blocks.text: If one task type makes up the vast majority of a multi-task dataset, the model can end up performing that task well at the expense of the others, which are underrepresented and therefore undertrained relative to what the dominant task received.

Deliberately balancing the number of examples per task, or weighting less represented tasks more heavily during training, helps prevent this kind of imbalance from quietly skewing the final model capability.

blocks.text: 4. Positive Transfer Between Related Tasks

blocks.alt: Training on related task A produces positive transfer that improves related task B too

blocks.text: When the tasks in a mixture are genuinely related, summarization and extraction, for instance, training on one can actually improve performance on the other, since the underlying skills, understanding and condensing text, overlap meaningfully between them.

blocks.title: This is transfer learning showing up again, at a smaller scale
blocks.content: The same underlying idea covered in the earlier Transfer Learning topic, that related skills reinforce each other, applies directly within a multi-task fine-tuning mixture, not just between pretraining and fine-tuning.

blocks.text: 5. Negative Transfer, When Tasks Interfere

blocks.alt: Training on conflicting task A produces negative transfer that hurts conflicting task B

blocks.text: Not every task combination helps each other, sometimes two tasks pull the model in genuinely conflicting directions, a task that rewards terse output mixed with one that rewards elaborate, detailed output, for example, and training on both together can measurably hurt performance on one or both relative to training on either alone.

Testing task combinations experimentally, rather than assuming any mixture will work well together, is the only reliable way to catch this kind of interference before it shows up in a deployed system.
6. Task Prefixes and Explicit Task Signaling

blocks.alt: A task prefix tag paired with the input tells the model which task it is handling

blocks.text: A common technique for multi-task datasets is prefixing each input with an explicit tag identifying which task it belongs to, summarize, classify, extract, giving the model a clear signal about which behavior is expected for that specific example, rather than relying on it to infer the task purely from context.
7. Evaluating Across Multiple Tasks at Once

blocks.alt: Evaluation runs separately across task A, task B, and task C

blocks.text: A multi-task fine-tuned model needs to be evaluated separately on each task it was trained for, since strong overall average performance can hide a real weakness on one specific task that a single blended metric would obscure.
8. Multi-Task vs Training Separate Models

blocks.alt: One multi-task model is compared against maintaining separate models per task

blocks.text: Multi-task fine-tuning trades some peak per task performance, since task specific fine-tuning generally reaches slightly deeper specialization, for the operational simplicity of deploying and maintaining just one model instead of several separate ones.
9. Choosing a Task Mixture Deliberately

The tasks included in a multi-task mixture should be chosen deliberately based on what a real deployed system actually needs, rather than combined simply because the data happened to be available, since an unnecessarily broad mixture increases both interference risk and evaluation overhead without a clear benefit.
Worked Example

A team building a single internal assistant that needs to summarize documents, extract key dates, and classify document type builds a multi-task dataset combining all three, using explicit task prefixes on every example and deliberately balancing example counts across the three task types.

After training, they evaluate each task separately and find summarization and extraction actually improved together, likely from positive transfer, while classification performed slightly below what a dedicated task specific model would have reached, an acceptable tradeoff given the operational simplicity of shipping one model instead of three.
Common Mistakes

items: Combining tasks into one mixture without checking for possible negative transfer between them
Letting one task dominate the dataset by example count, undertraining the others
Reporting only an overall average metric instead of evaluating each task in the mixture separately
Including a task in the mixture simply because data was available, rather than because the deployed system actually needs it

blocks.text: Practice

Take two or three tasks a real system might need, and consider whether they seem likely to help each other through positive transfer, summarization and extraction, for instance, or potentially conflict through negative transfer, terse classification and elaborate explanation, for instance.
Key Takeaway

Multi-task fine-tuning trains one model across several related tasks at once, trading some peak per task performance for operational simplicity, and doing it well requires balancing task representation, watching for both positive and negative transfer between tasks, and evaluating every task in the mixture separately rather than trusting a single blended score.
